## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/03.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">SMART Background
• Launched in May 2021, Idaho Striving to Meet Achievement in
Reading Together (SMART) is a multi-year cohort project training
K-3 educators in science-based reading instruction and
intervention.
• Participants engage in facilitated learning with Speech to Print by
Dr. Louisa Moats, guided implementation of evidence-based
practices, and coaching for sustained instructional improvement.
• The goal is to equip K-3 educators with science-aligned reading
strategies to improve student outcomes on the Idaho Reading
Inventory (IRI).</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/04.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">SMART: IRI Impact
• To investigate whether SMART benefits IRI outcomes, we
examine whether students learn more in SMART classrooms
than non-SMART classrooms.
• Using 2022-2023 and 2023-2024 IRI assessment results we
calculate the growth (i.e., learning) of students and compare
rates of learning between groups to examine SMART impact.
• NOTE: Simply comparing IRI outcomes between SMART and
non-SMART students can potentially provide misleading results
as students are not randomly-assigned to the SMART program.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/07.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Research Questions:
• Do students instructed by SMART participating teachers
demonstrate more learning (i.e., greater growth) than other
students.
• Does student growth/learning differ by grade of student/
teacher?
• Does student growth/learning differ by number of years of
teacher participation in SMART?
• Does student growth/learning differ by number of years of
student receiving SMART instruction?</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/08.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Background on Student Growth
• Calculation of student growth requires longitudinal, individual results from at least
two assessments (usually in the same content area administered at the same time).
• When thinking about student growth/learning, most users immediately think of
gain (i.e., change) scores.
• Calculation of change across two tests requires the test be scaled vertically placing
the results of both tests on the same scale.
• The IRI is vertically scaled.
• However, gain scores are not a viable growth model because student change is
dependent upon where a student starts.
• All defensible growth models utilize regression to accommodate dependency upon
where a student starts.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/09.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Student Growth Percentiles (SGPs)
• SGPs were derived to obviate issues related to the interpretation of change on score scales.
• The SGP properties I discuss are associated with those derived via the methodology
implemented in the SGP package for the R software environment.
• SGPs are integers ranging from 1 to 99 where 1st percentile growth is the lowest and 99th
percentile growth is the highest.
• SGPs are independent of prior achievement meaning that low and high achieving students
have the same chances of demonstrating low or high growth.
• SGPs utilize non-parametric (B-spline) based quintile regression to accommodate both non-
linearity of the multi-variate score distribution as well as heteroskedasticity.
• SGPs are invariant to mono-tone transformations of scale.
• In general, assessment changes resulting in the change of score scale do not impact the
calculation of SGPs (cohort referenced).</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/10.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">IRI Data
• For SGP calculations, IRI data was utilized from the 2022-2023
and 2023-2024 academic years.
• Fall and Spring IRI data was utilized to calculate Fall-to-
Spring SGPs in both 2022-2023 and 2023-2024
• Students with appropriate Fall and Spring scaled scores in
grade K, 1, 2, and 3 received SGPs.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/11.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Potential Issues related to SGPs and inferences
regarding SMART
• Because SGP calculations utilize scaled scores, properties of the scaled score
distribution can impact the results.
• Ceiling/Floor effects: SGPs model the multi-variate distribution and
attempt to model 99 conditional quantile curves based upon the scaled
score supplied. When the score distribution is capped and
disproportionate numbers of students are assigned HOSS/LOSS, SGPs will
be impacted.
• Inferences regarding SMART impact (using SGPs or any metric) are only as
good as the data on which they are based.
• If the IRI does not assess what SMART instruction teaches children, then
results from the IRI will not be sensitive to changes in those outcomes.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/13.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">SMART Participation
• IRI data for the 2022-2023 and 2023-2024 academic years was examined.
• At the start of 2022-2023, between 3.2% (Grade 3) and 5.3% (Grade 1)
students were associated with teachers participating in the SMART
program.
• At the start of 2023-2024, between 5.5% (Grade 3) and 11.7% (Grade
1) students were associated with teachers participating in the SMART
program.
• The achievement level of students participating in the program in
2022-2023 was slightly lower in 3 out of 4 grades and in 2023-2024 was
slightly lower in 1 out of 4 grades.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/15.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">SGP Calculation
• Though initial achievement level of students associated with SMART instruction was, in general,
comparable to those not associated with the program, we examine growth/learning by conditioning
upon prior (Fall) achievement.
• SGPs were calculated using IRI reading data supplied by IDOE for 2022-2023 and 2023-2024 in
grades K, 1, 2, and 3.
• SGPs were calculated for Fall-to-Spring in 2022-2023 and 2023-2024.
• SGPs for Spring 2023 utilized a Fall 2022 prior.
• SGPs for Spring 2024 utilized a Fall 2023 prior and Spring 2023 prior (if available)
• Due to the multi-week testing window associated with IRI administration, time between the spring
and fall administration was incorporated into the analyses to account for variability in time-lag
between test administration.
• Analyses were conducted using the R software environment (4.4.3) and the SGP package (2.2-1.93).
• All analyses ran without error and no technical issues emerged in the calculation of the SGPs.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/17.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">SGP Calculation: Goodness of Fit
• SGP results show excellent fit in both years and in all grades.
• No ceiling or floor effects were observed on any of the assessments.
• SGPs were uniformly distributed across all prior achievement levels.
• By definition, the mean/median of the SGPs (for the entire grade) is
• However, subgroups (e.g., students associated with SMART
instruction) can deviate from 50.
• Results above 50 indicate increased rates of learning/growth.
• Results below 50 indicate decreased rates of learning/growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/22.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">SGP Results
• In 2022-2023, Grades K and 2 showed statistically significant
increases in growth/learning.
• In 2023-2024, Grades K, 1, and 3 showed statistically significant
increases in growth/learning while Grade 2 showed a statistically
significant decrease.
• Though the results are statistically significant due to large sample
size, the results are not practically significant.
• Results based upon number of years participating in SMART mirror
the increases but do not show overall increases in learning with two
years participation over one year.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/32.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Instructor Level Performance
• In general, the results suggest broad variability in rates of
student learning associated with factors that extend beyond
the curriculum/pedagogy (SMART) being utilized.
• The slightly negative correlations suggest SMART instruction
is potentially of greater benefit to lower achieving students.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/33.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">SMART Impact by Prior Achievement
• The summary results suggest that student associated with SMART participants
demonstrated greater rates of learning if they were lower achieving.
• Discussions with IDE (Meghan) indicated that SMART emphasizes learning to
read over reading to learn which suggest greater efficacy for lower achieving
readers.
• To investigate this hypothesis, we examine student growth/learning of
students associated with SMART by prior achievement quintile.
• In some grades, the results, in general, indicate slightly better rates of learning
for lower achieving students.
• The following figures illustrate results for Grade 1, 2023-2024</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/48.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Conclusions
• I commend IDE for investigating the efficacy of the SMART program using IRI
data in “real time”.
• Overall, the results suggest, at best, modest improvement in student learning
for students/teachers in the SMART program.
• These results confirm, I think, some things that we all know:
• “Everything works somewhere. Nothing works everywhere.” Dylan Wiliam
• There are no silver bullets.
• There are likely numerous pedagogical factors beyond SMART participation at
play that also need to be addressed to substantially improve student rates of
learning.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/50.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

